landing:
What you will make

Make an alarm with a Raspberry Pi Pico. It will notice a change, give a warning, and let you reset it. What it watches and how it warns are your choices.

First open the starter project and complete connect and test your Pico. Once its LED and ready message work on your real Pico, choose any part:

  • Make its home: craft a case or adapt an object.
  • Detect a change: press, touch, tip, block light, move nearby and more. Choose one or several.
  • Give a warning: use a light, colours, a buzzer or a mixture.
  • Decide when: choose a trigger, add an arm switch, or change the warning pattern.
  • Bring it together: connect your chosen action to a warning, then test and reset it.

The page numbers group choices; they are not a list to complete in order. You can craft, wire or code first after the Pico check. If a page needs a part you have not tested, follow its link back and return. The alarm ideas at the end are examples to borrow from, not builds to copy.

options.title: Choose what counts as a trigger

1A.title: Connect and test your Pico
1A.html:
Connect and test your Pico

Everyone does this first. The starter checks the board before you choose any alarm parts.

Step 1

Try this

Download the starter project. Open it in Thonny and save your own copy as alarm.py.

Step 2

Try this

Connect your Pico with a USB data cable. In Thonny choose MicroPython (Raspberry Pi Pico) as the interpreter.

Step 3

Try this

Run your starter. Its first test is:

python
from picozero import pico_led
from time import sleep

pico_led.on()
sleep(1)
pico_led.off()
print("Pico and picozero are ready")

Test

Try this

Did the onboard LED light for one second? Did the Shell show Pico and picozero are ready? Keep your saved starter for the alarm you make.

Tip

If Thonny cannot find the Pico, check the USB data cable and interpreter. If it says No module named picozero, install picozero through Tools → Manage packages.

Choose a case, input, warning or rule next. You can change direction later.

2A.title: Follow your own alarm idea
2A.html:
Follow your own alarm idea

What change do you want to notice? A lid opening, a hand approaching, an object moving or something else?

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Do that before testing any circuit. You can sketch now and return.

Step 1

Try this

Finish this sentence: When ______ happens, my alarm will ______. Decide how someone will reset it.

Step 2

Try this

Try a quick shape or position. Leave room for the Pico, USB cable, input wires and warning light or buzzer. Keep the circuit removable while you test.

Test

Try this

Act out the trigger and the reset. Could another person tell when the alarm is armed and when it has warned them?

Choose any input in group 3 and any warning in group 4. Their pages have the wiring and code.

2B.title: Fold a home for it
2B.html:
Fold a home for it

Card and paper can hide the circuit or make the warning more visible.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Do that before testing the circuit. You can fold a model now.

Step 1

Try this

Fold a card case or stand. Mark where the input will sense a change and where someone can see or hear the warning.

Step 2

Try this

Leave an opening for the USB cable and a flap for fixing wires. Keep metal foil contacts apart until the action you want makes them meet.

Test

Try this

Can you reach the Pico without tearing the case? Can the input still sense what it needs to sense?

You can change the shape once the circuit works.

2C.title: Adapt an object
2C.html:
Adapt an object

A box, bag, model or toy can become the alarm's home.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Do that before testing the circuit. You can choose an object now.

Step 1

Try this

Pick an object and decide what change it should notice. Try the movement before fixing any electronics to it.

Step 2

Try this

Support the Pico on removable card. Keep the USB socket accessible. Cover any loose metal that could touch the circuit by accident.

Test

Try this

Move or open the object. Can you put the input where it will detect that change reliably?

Choose an input from group 3 and follow its diagram before attaching it permanently.

3A.title: Press or separate contacts
3A.html:
Press or separate contacts

A press or two pieces of foil meeting can tell an alarm that something opened or moved.

Before you test

First complete Connect and test your Pico. You can explore this idea before wiring it.

Step 1

Try this

Gather a push button or foil and a card spacer.

Connect GP10 through the switch to GND. A four-leg button has joined pairs: follow the picture.

Step 2

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import Button

button = Button(10)

pressed = button.is_pressed

Add this underneath to see when the component detects an event:

python
print(pressed)
if pressed:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Press and release. Run the code each time and look for True and False. Keep foil apart until pressed. Change the number or reverse the if condition if your alarm needs the opposite action.

Make it yours

A flap, lid or door can close your switch. When your test detects the event you want, join it to a warning.

3B.title: Touch a pad
3B.html:
Touch a pad

A light touch can trigger a secret alarm.

Before you test

First complete Connect and test your Pico. You can explore this idea before wiring it.

Step 1

Try this

Gather a TTP223 touch module and three leads.

SIG goes to GP17, VCC to 3V3 OUT, and GND to GND.

Step 2

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import TouchSensor

touch = TouchSensor(17)

touched = touch.is_touched

Add this underneath to see when the component detects an event:

python
print(touched)
if touched:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Touch and release the pad. A bare foil or thread contact uses the switch page instead. Change the number or reverse the if condition if your alarm needs the opposite action.

Make it yours

Hide the pad behind thin card, then test that it still detects touch. When your test detects the event you want, join it to a warning.

3C.title: Flip a switch
3C.html:
Flip a switch

A toggle can trigger the alarm or arm it.

Before you test

First complete Connect and test your Pico. You can explore this idea before wiring it.

Step 1

Try this

Gather an SPDT toggle switch and two leads.

Connect COM (centre leg) to GP6 and one outside leg to GND. Leave the other outside leg unconnected.

Step 2

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import Switch

mode = Switch(6)

mode_two = mode.is_closed

Add this underneath to see when the component detects an event:

python
print(mode_two)
if mode_two:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Flip the switch each way and run again. Use it to choose an armed mode. Change the number or reverse the if condition if your alarm needs the opposite action.

Make it yours

Use this as an arm switch on the arm and reset page, or treat a flipped switch as the event. When your test detects the event you want, join it to a warning.

3D.title: Tip or move it
3D.html:
Tip or move it

A tilt switch can notice when someone picks up or moves an object.

Before you test

First complete Connect and test your Pico. You can explore this idea before wiring it.

Step 1

Try this

Gather a ball tilt switch and two leads.

Connect GP8 through the switch to GND.

Step 2

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import Switch

tilt = Switch(8)

tilted = tilt.is_open

Add this underneath to see when the component detects an event:

python
print(tilted)
if tilted:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Tip slowly. The reading may flicker while the ball rolls. Change the number or reverse the if condition if your alarm needs the opposite action.

Make it yours

Place it inside a model treasure or prop that someone might move. When your test detects the event you want, join it to a warning.

3E.title: Watch the light
3E.html:
Watch the light

A shadow or sudden light can show that a cover has moved.

Before you test

First complete Connect and test your Pico. You can explore this idea before wiring it.

Step 1

Try this

Gather an LDR, a 10 kΩ resistor and leads.

Join the LDR and resistor at GP27. The LDR’s other leg goes to 3V3 OUT; the resistor’s other leg goes to GND.

Step 2

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import AnalogInputDevice

ldr = AnalogInputDevice(27)

light = ldr.value

Add this underneath to see when the component detects an event:

python
print(light)
if light < 0.5:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Cover and uncover it. With this wiring, darker gives a lower value. Change the number or reverse the if condition if your alarm needs the opposite action.

Make it yours

Hide it in a box to notice an opened lid: change < to > so light triggers it. When your test detects the event you want, join it to a warning.

3F.title: Notice someone nearby
3F.html:
Notice someone nearby

A distance sensor can notice an approaching hand without contact.

Before you test

First complete Connect and test your Pico. You can explore this idea before wiring it.

Step 1

Try this

Gather a 3.3 V-compatible HC-SR04P ultrasonic sensor and four leads.

Trig goes to GP20, Echo to GP21, VCC to 3V3 OUT and GND to GND. Use the HC-SR04P, not a 5 V Echo module.

Step 2

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import DistanceSensor

sensor = DistanceSensor(
    echo=21, trigger=20
)

distance = sensor.distance

Add this underneath to see when the component detects an event:

python
print(distance)
if distance is not None and distance < 0.3:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Move your hand in front of the two round parts. The number is metres; None means no echo. Change the number or reverse the if condition if your alarm needs the opposite action.

Make it yours

Choose how close someone must get before the warning starts. When your test detects the event you want, join it to a warning.

3G.title: Cross a marked line
3G.html:
Cross a marked line

A line sensor can detect a dark or light strip passing underneath.

Before you test

First complete Connect and test your Pico. You can explore this idea before wiring it.

Step 1

Try this

Gather a KY-033 line sensor, contrasting card and three leads.

S goes to GP18, V+ to 3V3 OUT and G to GND.

Step 2

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import DigitalInputDevice

line = DigitalInputDevice(18, pull_up=False)

on_line = line.is_active

Add this underneath to see when the component detects an event:

python
print(on_line)
if on_line:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Move a marked strip under the sensor. Adjust its small dial until the reading changes. Change the number or reverse the if condition if your alarm needs the opposite action.

Make it yours

Move a card tab with a drawer or door to reveal a new mark. When your test detects the event you want, join it to a warning.

3H.title: Turn a dial
3H.html:
Turn a dial

A dial can be a secret setting, a trigger or a sensitivity control.

Before you test

First complete Connect and test your Pico. You can explore this idea before wiring it.

Step 1

Try this

Gather a 10 kΩ potentiometer and three leads.

One end goes to GND, the middle to GP26, and the other end to 3V3 OUT. Check your dial’s leg order.

Step 2

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import Pot

pot = Pot(26)

setting = pot.value

Add this underneath to see when the component detects an event:

python
print(setting)
if setting > 0.5:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Turn gently. Run again at different positions; the value should move between about 0 and 1. Change the number or reverse the if condition if your alarm needs the opposite action.

Make it yours

Use it to choose the trigger distance or light level when you choose a trigger. When your test detects the event you want, join it to a warning.

3I.title: Notice warmth
3I.html:
Notice warmth

A temperature sensor can notice a slow change in warmth.

Before you test

First complete Connect and test your Pico. You can explore this idea before wiring it.

Step 1

Try this

Gather a TMP36 sensor and three leads.

Flat face towards you: left to 3V3, centre to GP28, right to GND. Keep the legs apart.

Step 2

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from picozero import TemperatureSensor

convert = lambda voltage: (voltage - 0.5) * 100
sensor = TemperatureSensor(28, conversion=convert)

temperature = sensor.temp

Add this underneath to see when the component detects an event:

python
print(temperature)
if temperature > 25:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Read the room temperature, then warm the sensor gently with your fingers. Change the number or reverse the if condition if your alarm needs the opposite action.

Make it yours

Use it for a warm/cool exhibit; set a threshold different from room temperature. When your test detects the event you want, join it to a warning.

3J.title: Check warm or cool
3J.html:
Check warm or cool

A sealed probe can compare warm and cool water slowly.

Before you test

First complete Connect and test your Pico. You can explore this idea before wiring it.

Step 1

Try this

Gather a sealed DS18B20 probe, a 4.7 kΩ resistor and leads.

VDD goes to 3V3, DQ to GP22, GND to GND. Put 4.7 kΩ between DQ and 3V3. Check your probe’s wire colours.

Step 2

Try this

Run the Skills Bricks code in Thonny:

python
from machine import Pin
import onewire, ds18x20
from time import sleep_ms

bus = onewire.OneWire(Pin(22))
sensor = ds18x20.DS18X20(bus)
probes = sensor.scan()
assert probes, "Check probe wiring"
sensor.convert_temp()
sleep_ms(750)
temperature = sensor.read_temp(probes[0])
print(temperature)

Add this underneath to see when the component detects an event:

python
if temperature > 25:
    print("Alarm trigger detected!")

Test

Try this

Wait for each new reading. Only the sealed tip goes in water; keep the Pico and connections dry. Change the number or reverse the if condition if your alarm needs the opposite action.

Make it yours

Make a warm/cool warning experiment; a probe needs time to change. When your test detects the event you want, join it to a warning.

4A.title: Flash one LED
4A.html:
Flash one LED

A single LED can give a bright, simple warning.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Unplug before wiring. Test the LED alone before adding an input.

Step 1

Try this

Use an LED and a 220 Ω resistor. Connect GP11 → resistor → long LED leg and short leg → GND. The resistor must stay in the circuit.

Step 2

Try this

Try the Skills Bricks LED code:

python
from picozero import LED

led = LED(11)

led.on()

Add led.off() after looking at it. In your alarm, if triggered: can turn the LED on; else: can turn it off.

Test

Try this

Did it light? If not, check which leg is long, the resistor, GP11 and GND. Try placing it where a player can see it.

4B.title: Change warning colours
4B.html:
Change warning colours

An RGB LED can show one colour for ready and another for warning.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Test the RGB LED alone before adding inputs. Use a common-cathode LED.

Step 1

Try this

Connect the R leg through 220 Ω to GP3, G through 220 Ω to GP4, B through 220 Ω to GP5, and the common long leg to GND. Each colour needs its own resistor.

Step 2

Try this

Try the Skills Bricks RGB LED code:

python
from picozero import RGBLED

light = RGBLED(red=3, green=4, blue=5)

light.color = (255, 0, 255)

Try light.color = (0, 255, 0) for ready and (255, 0, 0) for warning. Use light.off() to switch it off.

Test

Try this

Can you make two colours that someone can tell apart? Put a label or shape beside the light so colour is not the only clue.

4C.title: Sound an active buzzer
4C.html:
Sound an active buzzer

An active buzzer has one built-in pitch. You can change its beep rhythm. Check the packet for active or built-in oscillator.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Use a small 3.3 V GPIO-compatible buzzer and unplug before wiring.

Step 1

Try this

Connect buzzer + → GP9 and − → GND.

Step 2

Try this

Try the Skills Bricks active-buzzer code:

python
from picozero import Buzzer

buzzer = Buzzer(9)

buzzer.on()
from time import sleep
sleep(0.25)
buzzer.off()

In an alarm, if triggered: can turn it on; else: can turn it off.

Test

Try this

Did you hear one steady pitch? Change the length, not its pitch, to make the warning yours. An active buzzer cannot play different notes.

4D.title: Make a warning tone
4D.html:
Make a warning tone

A passive buzzer can change pitch. Check the packet for passive or external drive; it can look like an active buzzer.

Before you test

Have you completed Connect and test your Pico? Use one small 3.3 V GPIO-compatible piezo buzzer on GP9 at a time.

Step 1

Try this

Connect buzzer + → GP9 and − → GND.

Step 2

Try this

Try the Skills Bricks passive-buzzer code:

python
from picozero import PWMBuzzer

# GP9, 2000 Hz, 50% duty
buzzer = PWMBuzzer(9, 2000, 32768)

buzzer.on()
from time import sleep
sleep(0.25)
buzzer.off()

Change 2000 to 1000 before running again to hear a different pitch.

Test

Try this

Did the pitch change? If not, check whether you have an active buzzer. You can make a new warning pattern.

5A.title: Choose what counts as a trigger
5A.html:
Choose what counts as a trigger

Your alarm decides when a reading is enough to warn someone. Choose your own line.

Before you test

First test your Pico and test the input you want to use. A reading from an untested sensor can make the alarm seem broken.

Step 1

Try this

Here is the Skills Bricks light-sensor circuit. Read your own sensor in its usual place, then while you trigger it.

Step 2

Try this

Put your trigger value between those two readings. For an LDR wired as shown, darker usually gives a smaller number:

python
from picozero import AnalogInputDevice

ldr = AnalogInputDevice(27)
if ldr.value < 0.5:
    print("Too dark: warn someone!")

Use > to notice a lid opening into light. For another sensor, keep its wiring and reading from its page; change only the test inside if.

Test

Try this

Try the ordinary situation and the trigger three times each. Adjust 0.5 until the message appears only when you want it. Then join it to a warning.

5B.title: Arm and reset your alarm
5B.html:
Arm and reset your alarm

Add an arm switch so your alarm only watches for a trigger when you choose.

Before you test

First test your Pico, toggle switch, trigger input and warning. Unplug before joining circuits.

Step 1

Try this

Keep the Skills Bricks switch wiring: COM to GP6, one outside leg to GND.

Step 2

Try this

This example uses a button on GP10 and an LED on GP11. The warning stops when you disarm or release the button; that is its reset.

python
from picozero import Switch, Button, LED
from time import sleep

arm = Switch(6)
trigger = Button(10)
warning = LED(11)

while True:
    if arm.is_closed and trigger.is_pressed:
        warning.on()
    else:
        warning.off()
    sleep(0.05)

Test

Try this

Try all four combinations: armed/disarmed and button pressed/released. Decide whether your alarm should reset automatically like this, or need a separate reset action.

5C.title: Change the warning pattern
5C.html:
Change the warning pattern

A warning can flash or beep in a pattern you invent.

Before you test

First test your Pico, one input and one warning. Test a plain on/off warning when you join them before changing its rhythm.

Step 1

Try this

Keep the Skills Bricks LED circuit: GP11, a 220 Ω resistor, LED, then GND.

Step 2

Try this

This flashes only while a GP10 button is pressed. The short sleep lets the Pico check the button again quickly.

python
from picozero import Button, LED
from time import sleep

trigger = Button(10)
warning = LED(11)
lit = False

while True:
    if trigger.is_pressed:
        lit = not lit
        if lit:
            warning.on()
        else:
            warning.off()
        sleep(0.2)
    else:
        warning.off()
        lit = False
        sleep(0.05)

For sound, use a tested active or passive buzzer in place of the LED. Keep beeps short and comfortable.

Test

Try this

Try 0.1 and 0.5 seconds. Can someone tell when the alarm is warning? Does it stop soon after you reset it?

6A.title: Join one input and warning
6A.html:
Join one input and warning

Now make a first working alarm: notice something → warn → reset. This button-and-LED example is a starting point; swap in your choices.

Before you test

First test your Pico, input and warning separately. Unplug before combining wiring. Give each part its own GP pin.

Step 1

Try this

Wire the Skills Bricks button between GP10 and GND. Wire the LED from GP11 through a 220 Ω resistor to its long leg, then its short leg to GND. The circuits share GND.

Step 2

Try this

Add this below the starter test in your saved alarm.py:

python
from picozero import Button, LED
from time import sleep

trigger = Button(10)
warning = LED(11)

while True:
    if trigger.is_pressed:
        warning.on()
    else:
        warning.off()
    sleep(0.05)

For your own parts, keep their exact setup and reading from their Skills Bricks pages. Put your condition after if, and your warning action inside it.

Test

Try this

Press: warning on. Release: warning off. That release is the reset. If yours warns at the wrong time, swap the if condition or adjust its threshold.

6B.title: Add another input or warning
6B.html:
Add another input or warning

One input and one warning are enough. Add a second part only if it improves your idea.

Before you test

First make one input and warning work. Test every new part on its own. Unplug before changing wiring; check that the GP pins do not clash.

Step 1

Try this

This example adds a tilt switch on GP8 and an active buzzer on GP9 to a button on GP10 and LED on GP11. Use the wiring from each Skills Bricks page.

Step 2

Try this

or makes either input trigger both warnings:

python
from picozero import Button, Switch, LED, Buzzer
from time import sleep

button = Button(10)
tilt = Switch(8)
light = LED(11)
sound = Buzzer(9)

while True:
    if button.is_pressed or tilt.is_open:
        light.on()
        sound.on()
    else:
        light.off()
        sound.off()
    sleep(0.05)

Change or to and only if both events should be needed. If you chose another component, use its reading from its page.

Test

Try this

Try each input alone, then both together. Move the tilt back and release the button to reset. If it keeps warning, check which position makes tilt.is_open true.

7A.title: Try it and improve it
7A.html:
Try it and improve it

Let someone else test your alarm without showing them how it works first.

Before you test

Have you connected and tested the Pico and made one complete alarm? Finish those before judging the whole design.

Step 1

Try this

Show your tester how to arm or reset it. Ask them to trigger it three times. Watch for: a missed trigger, a false warning, a warning they cannot notice, or a hard-to-reach reset.

Step 2

Try this

Change one thing: position, threshold, wiring, code or warning pattern. The Skills Bricks button and LED diagrams are here if you need to retrace the first example.

python
if trigger.is_pressed:
    warning.on()
else:
    warning.off()

Test

Try this

Run the same three tests again. What improved? If a false warning remains, adjust where the sensor sits or the condition after if.

Note

Give your alarm a name and show which choice made it yours.

8A.title: Guard a model treasure
8A.html:
Guard a model treasure

Borrow this idea, change it, or ignore it. A model chest could warn when its lid opens.

Before you test

Complete the Pico test, then test the foil contact and LED before joining them.

Step 1

Try this

Put one foil contact on the lid and one on the box so they meet when shut. Treat them like the Skills Bricks button: one to GP10, one to GND. Add an LED and 220 Ω resistor on GP11.

Step 2

Try this

Start with this idea from the downloadable example:

python
from picozero import Button, LED
from time import sleep

lid = Button(10)
warning = LED(11)
while True:
    if not lid.is_pressed:  # foil contacts are apart
        warning.on()
    else:
        warning.off()
    sleep(0.05)

Test

Try this

Close the lid, then lift it. The LED should warn when contacts separate. If the contacts do not meet reliably, move them or add a small card flap. What else could a pair of contacts watch?

8B.title: Notice a visitor
8B.html:
Notice a visitor

Borrow this idea for a model shop, doorway or secret exhibit: warn when a hand gets close.

Before you test

Complete the Pico test, then test the 3.3 V-compatible distance sensor and RGB LED separately. Do not use a 5 V Echo pin on a Pico GPIO.

Step 1

Try this

Use the Skills Bricks circuits: sensor trigger GP20, echo GP21; RGB LED GP3/4/5 with one resistor per colour.

Step 2

Try this

This downloadable example uses green for ready and red when something is within 30 cm:

python
from picozero import DistanceSensor, RGBLED
from time import sleep

sensor = DistanceSensor(echo=21, trigger=20)
light = RGBLED(red=3, green=4, blue=5)
while True:
    distance = sensor.distance
    if distance is not None and distance < 0.3:
        light.color = (255, 0, 0)
    else:
        light.color = (0, 255, 0)
    sleep(0.1)

Test

Try this

Approach from different angles. Does 30 cm work for your design? Change 0.3 after checking what the sensor actually reads.

8C.title: Notice a moved object
8C.html:
Notice a moved object

Borrow this idea for a model artefact that complains when someone picks it up.

Before you test

Complete the Pico test, then test the tilt switch and active buzzer separately. Use a small 3.3 V GPIO-compatible buzzer.

Step 1

Try this

Connect the tilt switch between GP8 and GND, and the active buzzer + to GP9 and − to GND.

Step 2

Try this

The downloadable example sounds while the switch is open:

python
from picozero import Switch, Buzzer
from time import sleep

tilt = Switch(8)
warning = Buzzer(9)
while True:
    if tilt.is_open:
        warning.on()
    else:
        warning.off()
    sleep(0.05)

Test

Try this

Move and replace the object. The switch can rattle, so find a position where it is settled when the object rests. Do you want the opposite angle to be the trigger?
